utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There are no preliminaries. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness? And we'll hear that witness through a videolink. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that everything's fine, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear this -- the testimony of the witness, Witness GRM010, with protective measures of pseudonym, voice and face distortion. Can we verify whether the videolink is functioning well?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] From videolink's site we can hear you and we can see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We see some of you -- some but not all, but we can hear you clearly. Could you please inform me, Madam Registrar at the our side of the videolink, who is in the room with you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Apart from myself and the witness, there is ITSS technician as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. Witness, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, before you give evidence the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. Therefore, would you please repeat my words: I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness GRM010, because that's how we will call you, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Witness, if there would be any matter, any answer you intend to give which would reveal your identity, please ask to go into private session, because no one will see your face, no one will hear your voice, and we'll not use your own name. But if by answering a question you are at risk to reveal your identity, we'll move into private session so as to hear your answer without anyone else outside this courtroom hearing it. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you're ready, you may proceed. Mr. McCloskey, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honour. I'm -- don't know if you have the same, but we are not seeing the actual face. We're getting the face distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, face distortion is one of the protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I thought normally we didn't have to do that, and I think -- I thought we were able to actually be able to see the face and I think that's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed that this creates some technical problems because, of course, we're hearing this witness at long distance and that makes the difference compared to having a witness here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I now -- I now can see -- see the witness so I -- I take it that's not going to be a problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's always of some concern if the Prosecution sees more than the Judges do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I won't say we're all-knowing, but I hope you can see the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that by -- we have the left down button which can be activated only in this courtroom which allows us to see the witness, whereas on the record his face will be blurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go into private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends in the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the witness to be provided with 65 ter 1D05305. The document shouldn't be broadcast outside of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then I would kindly ask the witness not to read the document aloud but just to confirm whether the information contained in the document is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, shall we -- we move into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell the Chamber whether you gave a statement to the General Mladic Defence team, did you give that statement in writing, and did you answer all the questions that were put to you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, again without the document being broadcast out of the courtroom, I would like to call up 65 ter 1D01738. Once again, I would like to emphasise that the document shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember that you gave a statement to the Mladic Defence team and do you remember that you could then read it or listen to it being read out to you and that then you signed it as your own statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The B/C/S version has disappeared again. We should have the document in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We started both in B/C/S. Now we are in both English. We would appreciate to have one side in B/C/S, the other side in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the technical service for their help. And again, can we look at the last page of the statement in B/C/S and in English without broadcasting it outside of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness -- just a moment. Bear with me while we are waiting for the last page of the document to appear in English as well. Having read out the content of the statement, did you put your signature on the last page of this statement and could you please tell us when you did that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in paragraph 10 of this statement. Paragraph 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move a paragraph, the last question you put to the witness should be answered: "Tell us when you did that." And the witness only said "yes," but he has not given the time and the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear the question put to you by His Honour Judge Fluegge. Could you please read or could you please tell us if you remember the date when you signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date. No, no, I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. However, did you actually put the date on the day when you signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's look at paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, the document shouldn't be broadcast outside of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll direct your attention to the paragraph by actually reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for the Trial Chamber, I am directing you, Your Honours, to the last sentence where it says: "I let the soldier go. That soldier introduced himself to me as Milenko Mladic. After that I have never seen him."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, during the proofing session, did you actually voice your suspicion about the accuracy of the person's name? Did you share your dilemma with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: Yes. It is possible that his name was not Milenko but Milanko, but this is just the way I am thinking. And now I did not manage to get to the bottom of that. I'm sure that his last name is Mladic, but I'm not sure about his first name. I'm not sure whether he is Milenko or Milanko.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 11 in the last sentence of that paragraph, you voiced the same dilemma about the name referred to in paragraph 11; again, Milenko or Milanko.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's look at paragraph 19 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without broadcasting that part of the document outside of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In line 8 in the English version of the document and in line 6 of the B/C/S version, you mentioned that there were not more than 10 to 15 soldiers in that company. I don't want to identify the location. Did you tell me that you had some reservations about the number of people who were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: Yes. I counted the elements of that unit. However, again I didn't get to the bottom of that. There was the commander of that unit. There was a paramedic, and there were also five or six other men there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, instead of not more than 10 to 15 soldiers, what should state here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: I would add the number six plus one, and it would be a total of seven; right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And now that you have given the solemn declaration to speak the truth, and to the best of your recollection, now that you have made the two corrections to the statement, could you please tell the Trial Chamber whether today, under the oath, you claim that the statement reflects what you remember and what you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I tender 1D01738 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the formula is that we also ask the witness whether he would give the same answers if the same questions would be put to him today. Witness, have you heard what I just said? Would you give, in substance, the same answers if asked the same questions today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have one other question to you at this moment. You just discussed paragraph 19 and you said there must have been six plus one; so, therefore, seven soldiers. In paragraph 19 you are commenting on a report. Now, could you tell us where exactly you were when the events described in the report happened in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 10th to 21st, I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you did not personally observe what happened in Konjevic Polje and how many men there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you are also apparently aware of part of the unit being in Derventa. You were not in Derventa either at that time, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore your calculation of how many men would have been there is just on basis of what exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I base my calculation on my knowledge of previous orders and my knowledge of the unit that was located there. So those seven people were from the unit that was permanently based there, whereas parts of some other parts (redacted) were there just in transit. They went from there to complete assignments elsewhere. So this unit was permanently based there. It had those seven people as its members, the seven people that I have mentioned. So that was the maximum number. That was my estimate of its maximum strength based on what I knew who was registered as member of that unit. So it could have been fewer people than what I said but not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How could you exclude reinforcement or how could you exclude that those in transit may have assisted for a short while?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't actually exclude that. The figure I gave you pertains to the logistics unit that was based there. So I'm sure that figure is accurate in the sense that it could not have been more than that. As for the units that were in transit through the area, those were two units that passed through Konjevic Polje, and regarding them I said that in my estimate it could have been that number as a maximum number, knowing the assignments that the unit had and knowing its strength.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's all theory and how many people there actually were you are unable to tell us on the basis of your own observation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, meaning that you are, indeed, not able to tell it on the basis of your own observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This repeats the problem. When you say no, you mean that you indeed are not in a position to tell us what actually -- how many men there actually were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm not in the position to tell you exactly how many people there were actually there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. No objections. Madam, Registrar, the statement would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number 1D01738 receives exhibit number D846, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D846 is admitted, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission I would like to read the witness's summary. But prior to that, could we briefly go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll continue, Your Honour. The first tasks for this witness, when he found himself in the Sarajevo theatre of war, were construction works on the Lukavica-Pale road. He was then involved in erecting barricades around the Lukavica barracks and erecting shelters around the barracks. The first combat that the unit had was near the Vrbanja bridge. That's when they hit an ambush while they were providing security for the road taken by the JNA column which was leaving Sarajevo. He provides a lot of details about the event when he was assigned to camouflage and make shelters in Grbavica. He toured the positions with a MUP officer. Those positions were exposed to snipers. On that occasion, he personally heard a conversation over the radio between a member of the MUP of Republika Srpska and an unknown person in Pofalici. On that occasions, fire support was requested for the part of Pofalici inhabited by Serbs because a gang had started torching houses and plundering property. That's why the Serbs started withdrawing towards the Zuc and Mijatovici Kosa facilities. He remembers that on that occasion he met a member of his unit whose name was either Milenko or Milanko Mladic. He was in tears when he told him that from the positions where he was deployed he could hear smoke coming from the torched houses in Pofalici. One of those houses was the house of the Mladic family. On that same day, he also heard a radio communication between two collocutors who said that fire should be opened on Pofalici. As far as he remembers, the word used on that occasion were there are no longer any Serbs there anyway. He concluded that the request was made to open fire on either military or paramilitary formations who had chased the Serbian population from Pofalici. Your Honours, I would stop here and I would not go on reading the summary because the text could identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And with that, I would like to thank the witness for answering our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness GRM010, you'll now be cross-examined. Carefully listen to the questions. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, I first want to ask you about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I should have introduced you first. But perhaps you do it yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, you may remember me from many years ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- if you just say that you're Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- when I questioned you in another case. My name is Peter McCloskey. Now, I want to take you briefly to your time in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to D846.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where you talk about General Mladic speaking to people, including yourself, about Operation Lukavica 93. And on that, on page -- on paragraph 13 of your statement, you state: "On that occasion, he also explicitly said that the idea which was in many people's heads of capturing the city of Sarajevo, like cutting the aforementioned access ..." And that was, as you said earlier, the Grbavica-Tito barracks-Pofalici axis. And I'll -- by cutting the aforementioned axis was, and I quote, "unacceptable to him because it would cause many civilian casualties on both sides and would contribute to nothing but bloodshed." And you say: "This idea never again made it to the operational level or even the tactical level." Now are you saying, Witness, that Mladic after this time never intended to take over the Sarajevo city?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: I don't know what his intentions were. What I witnessed was that meeting and at that meeting he spoke about the objectives of Lukavica 93 operation. Amongst other things, he gave an explanation which I shared with you in the statement. Before that gathering, he --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't know what his intentions were regarding the Lukavica 93 operation regarding the potential take-over of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: At that meeting and in the documents that I had an occasion to see, I did not hear that or saw or see anything that would point to that. When he provided the explanation about that operation, he said that his idea was to take that area and to link up two corps, the Herzegovina and Sarajevo Romanija Corps. And as a result of those military successes, the enemy side would be forced to negotiate and a just peace would be achieved as a result of that. That's what he said. Those were his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P6549.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a document dated 26 June 1993. It's an order from General Galic, who we know was the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps at the time. This order is entitled: "Lukavac 93" as we would see on the first page of that order. And I'm not going to take you through this order completely, but does this look like an order that you would have received? Can you look at this order, sir? Can you see it on a screen or ...?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could relevant portions be read to the witness if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I'm sure Mr. Stojanovic would agree with me that this is the order that I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the first paragraph -- the second part of the first paragraph, it says: "It is expected that UNPROFOR forces will indirectly support the Muslims in their coming operations, and it is also possible that NATO forces will provide them direct air support." So, Witness, is it fair to say that General Mladic and General Galic would have considered the presence and potential activity of UNPROFOR and NATO in determining their intent towards the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: The meeting that I mentioned and where I heard what I heard and shared with you in the statement, there were no such stories at that meeting. I did not have an opportunity to attend any other meetings where that matter would have been discussed in that way and where a possibility that you've just mention would have been discussed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you answer the questions, the -- the witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GRM010
utterances.text: The answer is no. No, not in the sense that I did not have an occasion to attend such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We take the break a little bit earlier than usual. We'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00. And most likely we'll, although perhaps very briefly, then return into private session. We take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, you know that that's not what you're supposed to do. Would you refrain from doing that. Mr. McCloskey, are you ready to continue and should we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. President. I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into -- well, that's an answer to one of my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and yes, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So do -- you're -- and ready and we should move into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We take a break of 20 minutes and the expectation is that after the break we'll have another 10 to 15 minutes in private session. Mr. McCloskey, is that to be expected?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think so given the documents and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I just in order to inform the public about what the public can expect. We take a break and will resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, we return into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if we could go back briefly to P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We take a break and we resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I think we can remain in open session at this moment. I'd like to you ask -- no, let me first -- let's first turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Witness, I'd like to thank you very much for coming to the place where the videolink took place and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Chamber, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can terminate the videolink. Videolink ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness because we would have 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the next witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, for your information, the information on the Drina Corps collection was provided on one page of the transcript by Erin Gallagher a long time back. It can be found on transcript 9432 and 9433 and confirms the date I'd mentioned, but there's a bit more information. It's a unique situation. And also to let you know, Ms. Hasan is aware of an assignment -- a question you had about her witness, 130, about similar orders to a -- to one -- I think it was an order on the 15 July that you heard about and we are ready -- she's ready to respond briefly to that. We wanted to speak to Mr. Ivetic about what -- what we had found and we will do that and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would then ask to be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I assume that you're Mr. Amidzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Amidzic, before you give evidence the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Amidzic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You find him to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps if I could have the assistance of the usher, I have a hard copy of the statement which should allow us to go quicker and use our time efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The usher will certainly assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, good day, Colonel. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Bosko Amidzic. My father's name was Risto.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at this time I would call up in e-court 65 ter 1D01712.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, what we have on the screen you also have in front of you on paper. I would direct you to the Serbian original and ask you to tell us whose signature we see here on this first page.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC
utterances.text: On the first page, I can see my signature, my own signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can please turn to the last page of the Serbian original in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if could you turn to the last page of the hard copy that has been provided to you, can you tell us whose signature appears with the date on this page?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC
utterances.text: Also mine. My signature appears again, and the date is 25th June 2014. That's my personal signature in my own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you, in fact, recall giving a statement to the Defence team of General Mladic on the date which is indicated?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC
utterances.text: I remember that. That statement was read to me, and at that moment after the statement was read to me, I signed it in my own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now after you signed this statement, did you have an occasion this last week to re-read the whole statement in Serbian so as to check if everything is accurately recorded within the statement?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had that occasion. I read the entire statement, and I did make some corrections. I did make some changes to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to first turn to page 7 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to look together at paragraph number 29 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC
utterances.text: It says here: "On the 6th of June 1992, I dealt with eight specific issues." The mistake is instead of "eight" it should be "in addition to" or "besides" or "apart from."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to look at paragraph 32 on this same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, in English, this paragraph, 32, says that there were several camps for prisoners of war that were organised by your units; whereas, the Serbian says that there were no more such camps. Which is the correct fact?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC
utterances.text: It is correct that in my units or, rather, in my corps there was only one prisoner of war camp, and that was -- that one was in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to turn to page 12 in the English, page 13 in the Serbian, and I'd like to focus on paragraph number 63.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I would ask you simply to explain for us what clarification or correction is necessary to make this paragraph accurate.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, it says: "I was with him in Sanski Most." However, this should be corrected and this should read: "I was not with him in Sanski Most. General Vladic popped over to see me in Banja Luka, he read his every report to me," and the rest is correct. The rest of the paragraph reads: "If I had any objections I could share those with him. If not, then fine." In any case, what I wanted to correct was the fact that I did not accompany him to the assembly meeting in Sanski Most. That's the change.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can go to the next page in Serbian and page 14 in the English and paragraph 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the English, the date for these events in paragraph 64 is 1998, whereas in Serbian it is 1988. Can you tell us which date is accurate for the events in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC
utterances.text: The exact date or rather the exact year in my version is 1988. That's when the military was reorganised and the changes apply to that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, apart from these corrections and clarifications, do you stand by everything else in your written statement as written?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC
utterances.text: Everything that is written in this statement remains as is, and I stand by the form and the significance of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Colonel, if I were to ask you questions today arising out of the same topics as in your statement, would your answers to those questions be the same as we find in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC
utterances.text: They would always be the same. The next time, and I don't know how many times after that, were to you repeat the questions for -- from the statement, my answers would still be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, insofar as you have taken a solemn declaration to tell the truth, does that mean that your answers are truthful in nature, as recorded in the statement?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The answers are truthful, and indeed that's what they should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence would tender 1D01712 as a public exhibit. There are no associated exhibited with this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask the witness one question before admission of the statement. In relation to your correction you just made in paragraph 32, in June of this year, 25th of June, you signed this statement. There it reads: "There were several camps for prisoners of war reorganised by our units." Now you read that again, and you say: "There were no more camps for prisoners of war." What -- what -- what triggered this change? Why didn't you realise if that was a mistake, this mistake already in June of this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the difference is in the English. That did not -- the English translation came after the Serbian original, so that would not have been before the witness in June when he signed the Serbian original which does not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please read paragraph 32 which is on the screen at the moment in your language? Just this one sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly. Paragraph 32 reads: "There were no other prisoner of war camps in the organisation of our units." That what I'm reading and that's correct, full stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01712 receives exhibit number D847, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D847 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I at this time have a short public summary, which I think we could finish before the pause. The witness is a career military officer. When the VRS was established, he was chief of the quartermaster service within the 1st Krajina Corps. He was appointed assistant commander for logistics in February 1993. He retired from service in 1997. In 1993 the combat readiness analysis of the VRS concluded the VRS operated in extreme shortage of financial and material means and fuel, and very scarce material reserves at all levels. The war brought a disruption of the production structures, such that they were far from meeting the regular needs of the army and the population. The Operation Corridor 92 was undertaken because there was not enough food, medicines, and fuel, neither for the army nor the population. As to prisoners of war camps, the witness states that the only one organised by the 1st Krajina Corps was Manjaca, which only operated till November 1992 when the prisoners of war were exchanged. Prior to that time, the prisoners themselves prepared and distributed their own food. The witness states that many lies have been reported about Manjaca. The witness talks of the reception of Croats from Central Bosnia who were running from the Muslim forces in Central Bosnia and who were accommodated by the VRS, given food, water, and medical attention, and transported to destinations of their choice, upon order of General Mladic. This completes the summary of the witness, and I see that we're just about at the time for the break today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we finish, sir, can you look at page 84, line 11. Did you did you "disruption of the protection structures" or "production structures"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hope I said "production structures," that's what I meant. If I misspoke, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Amidzic, we will adjourn for the day. You've been with us only for a very short time, but we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning. But before you leave this courtroom, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever it may be, with -- about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today, not much yet although the whole statement is now in evidence, or whether that is evidence still to be given tomorrow. We'd like to see you back 9.30, tomorrow morning, in this same courtroom. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 9th of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of December, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.15 p.m.,
